newsitem.title: FRANCE: No silver lining in French election cloud.
newsitem.headline: No silver lining in French election cloud.

text.p: When French President Jacques Chirac called an early parliamentary election, many saw it as a risky gamble to clear away opposition to reform in a country he himself has condemned as conservative.

But as the campaign shapes up, economists say that if the centre right wins, the signs are pointing to a continuation of the same policies of tinkering with the budget deficit and taxation with the same result of weak growth and mass unemployment.
"I thought this was going to be a straight liberalism versus socialism election" Merrill Lynch economist Joanne Perez said.

"When the campaign was first announced it was meant to herald change. Since then the right has backed off. There is a feeling we have retrenched back to the old Juppe government line," she said, referring to Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
The election call may even have worsened the picture.

New investment, desperately needed to underpin a still fragile economic recovery, has been delayed yet again by the uncertainty created by the May 25 and June 1 vote -- and may be delayed further until the new government's policies emerge fully in the autumn.
That in turn could mean unemployment, now a record 12.8 percent, does not start coming down until well into next year.
"Already as a result of calling the election you have probably lowered growth this year," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
And against that background of low growth and joblessness, the government will have to impose new austerity in 1998 to keep the deficit low ahead of European monetary union in 1999.
"One way or another they are going to have to tighten fiscal policy after the election. That will be bad for growth," Williams said.

And while radical pruning of state spending could produce higher growth, France's gradualist approach was depressing domestic demand, lowering tax revenues and making the task of reducing the deficit even harder. "What France has done over the past few years is just awful," he said.

In the short-term the economy might gain from Socialist policies to stimulate demand, while in the longer term liberal policies to free the economy would boost growth, Perez said. "Taking a midway stance is neither helping one nor the other."

At the outset, Chirac's call for an early election seemed meant to attack that very problem -- lifting the country out of a paralysis where the threat of social unrest and deep-rooted conservatism forced his government into a middle path that merely marked time and kept France on course for monetary union.

One senior source said Chirac had become impatient with the slow pace of reform and wanted a clear hand not just to cut the deficit but also to carry out a slew of changes in the way the French state and its labour markets are run.
But with the free-market rhetoric which was seen early in the campaign now toned down, it will be hard for him to claim a mandate to do that after the election.

And imposing it afterwards could expose the government to accusations of making false campaign pledges -- provoking exactly the kind of anger and disillusionment that ran through the paralysing public sector strikes that broke out less than six months after Chirac own presidential election in 1995.
Then Juppe was forced to backtrack on many of his reforms.

Short of a change of prime minister -- seen as possible but uncertain given that Juppe has been running the campaign -- economists do not see a new government making the 1995 mistakes again. And if it does, it could be forced to backtrack again.
"There is a lot of danger in the right in that they haven't come clean about how far their reforms would go," Credit Lyonnais senior bond analyst Iain Lindsay said.
If opinion polls pointing to a narrow centre-right victory are to be believed, the goverment will be working with a sharply reduced parliamentary majority.

That in itself is not a problem in France, where the National Assembly wields far less influence than say in Britain. But the government's political standing, and its ability to face down social unrest, could be diminished.
"If the conservatives win, it seems it is going to be a narrower majority," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard.
"There is going to be a sense of non-achievement, of disappointment. It's half a defeat and all the problems are still there," he added.
